I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Background and Purpose — More information on the Annual LIHEAP Report to Congress.

Each year, the Office of Community Services publishes the LIHEAP Report to Congress, as required by Section 2610(a)(4) and (5) and section 2610(b) of the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program Act (42 U.S.C. 8629).

The LIHEAP Report to Congress provides information regarding the following:
• Sources and uses of LIHEAP funding
• Amount, cost and type of fuels used by LIHEAP eligible households
• Type of fuel used by various income groups
• Number and income levels of households assisted with LIHEAP
• Household LIHEAP benefit levels
• LIHEAP offset of average heating costs
• Number of LIHEAP assisted households that include vulnerable members
• LIHEAP recipiency targeting performance measures

Data for this report are collected from a variety of sources. For example, fiscal data is obtained from the Office of Community Services, while data regarding LIHEAP assisted households is compiled from grant recipient reports. Other data sources include the American Community Survey and Residential Energy Consumption Survey. More information regarding data collection activities can be found in Appendix A of each Report to Congress.

Information from the Report to Congress is used for Congressional oversight and in response to Congressional and White House queries. Data included in the Report to Congress can also be accessed through the Data Warehouse.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this federal dataset thoroughly. Let me start by gathering information from multiple angles.I'm gathering more details on the program's history, data warehouse, and recent developments.Let me get details on the Data Warehouse, the Report to Congress, and the performance measures structure.Let me verify a few final details: the current status of LIHEAP staffing/data continuity, and the most recent Report to Congress.# Comprehensive Research Report: LIHEAP Program Data

**Verification note:** Your description is accurate. The dataset exists as described. One nuance worth stating up front: "LIHEAP data" is not a single dataset but a *family* of related data collections, reports, and web tools administered by the Office of Community Services (OCS) within the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The report below treats the whole data ecosystem.

---

## 1. Overview: What the Data Is

LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program) is a federal block grant—approximately **$4.1 billion in FY2024**—that helps roughly **5.9–6.2 million low-income households** per year pay home heating and cooling bills, respond to energy crises (e.g., utility shutoffs), and fund low-cost weatherization. The data collection tracks:

- **Sources and uses of funds** by grant recipient (states, DC, tribes, tribal organizations, territories)
- **Household counts** (unduplicated) by assistance type: heating, cooling, crisis, weatherization
- **Household demographics**: poverty level intervals; presence of members aged 60+, members with disabilities, and young children (age 5 and under); owner/renter status
- **Benefit levels** (average benefit per household, by type of assistance)
- **Income eligibility cutoffs** (maximum income for a four-person household)
- **Performance measures**: energy burden targeting, restoration of home energy service, prevention of service loss
- **Home energy data**: fuel types, costs, and consumption by income group (drawn partly from other federal surveys)

### Core data products

| Product | Description |
|---|---|
| **LIHEAP Household Report** | Annual grantee-submitted counts of applicant and assisted households, by poverty interval and vulnerable population, separately for each assistance type |
| **LIHEAP Performance Data Form (LPDF)** | Annual report with Module 1 (Grantee Survey: funds, benefits, income cutoffs), Module 2 (required performance measures), Module 3 (optional measures) |
| **LIHEAP Report to Congress** | Annual published compilation (most recent posted: FY2022) with supplemental tables and Appendix A methodology |
| **LIHEAP Data Warehouse** | Interactive web tool (data since FY2001) with Standard Reports, Custom Reports, Grant Recipient Profiles (1-page state snapshots), and a Grantee Search Portal; CSV downloads available |
| **Home Energy Notebooks** | Periodic in-depth analyses of LIHEAP and low-income energy data |
| **LIHEAP Clearinghouse** | Companion site (liheapch.acf.gov) with program/policy information, state plan tables, and the National Energy Assistance Referral (NEAR) service |

---

## 2. Publisher and Administrative Chain

- **Publishing agency:** Administration for Children and Families (ACF), HHS
- **Administering office:** Office of Community Services (OCS), **Division of Energy Assistance (DEA)**
- **Key contractor:** **APPRISE Incorporated** (Applied Public Policy Research Institutes for Study and Evaluation), which reviews grantee reports, runs training webinars, prepares performance measurement reports, and supports the Data Warehouse
- **Reporting entities:** 50 states + DC (full reporting), plus tribes, tribal organizations, and territories (abbreviated reporting; tribes/territories do not file the Performance Data Form)
- **Submission system:** ACF's **Online Data Collection (OLDC)** system, part of Grant Solutions
- **Key URLs:** liheappm.acf.gov (Performance Management site + Data Warehouse), liheapch.acf.gov (Clearinghouse), acf.gov/ocs

---

## 3. Statutory Authority and Reporting Mandate

LIHEAP data collection is not discretionary—it is written into the statute:

- **Authorizing law:** The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Act of 1981, Title XXVI of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 (P.L. 97-35), codified at **42 U.S.C. §§ 8621–8630**.
- **§ 2610 (42 U.S.C. § 8629) — Data Collection:** Directs the HHS Secretary, after consultation with the Secretary of Energy, to collect data on home energy consumption; amount/cost/type of fuels used by eligible households; fuel type by income group; number and income levels of assisted households; and counts of assisted households with elderly, disabled, or young-child members. **§ 2610(b)** requires the Secretary to submit a report to Congress **no later than June 30 each year** covering the prior fiscal year, including how states carried out key program requirements and each state's program impact.
- **§ 2605(c)(1)(G)** (as amended by § 309 of the Human Services Amendments of 1994, P.L. 103-252): Requires grant recipients to report, as part of their annual grant application, the number and income levels of households applying for and receiving assistance, including vulnerable-population breakdowns.
- **Implementing regulation:** **45 CFR Part 96, Subpart H**, esp. **§ 96.82** — states and large insular areas must submit household data with their grant application for the prior federal fiscal year, broken out by heating, cooling, crisis, and weatherization; smaller insular areas and tribes report simpler counts. Critically, **grantees do not receive their LIHEAP allotment until the report is received**—a strong compliance mechanism that keeps the data series nearly complete.
- **Reauthorization:** The Energy Policy Act of 2005 (P.L. 109-58, Subtitle B) reauthorized LIHEAP through FY2007; the program has operated since on continuing appropriations, and reauthorization remains pending.
- **OMB clearances (Paperwork Reduction Act):** Household Report — OMB Control No. **0970-0060**; Performance Data Form — OMB Control No. **0970-0449**. Both require periodic renewal via Federal Register notice, which creates public comment opportunities.
- **Cross-agency data sharing:** The statute explicitly allows HHS to use data collected by other agencies; the Report to Congress supplements grantee reports with the Census Bureau's **American Community Survey** and EIA's **Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS)**.

### Reporting calendar (current cycle)

- Household Report: preliminary data due ~**October 15**, final due **December 31** (with grant application)
- Performance Data Form: due **January 31** (states + DC only)
- Report to Congress: statutory deadline June 30 for the prior FY (in practice, publication often lags several years—the most recent posted report covers FY2022)

---

## 4. History of the Program and Its Data

- **1975–1979 — Predecessor crisis programs:** The Emergency Energy Conservation Program (P.L. 93-644, administered by the Community Services Administration) began in 1975 with ~$16.5M, focused on weatherization. After the severe 1976–77 winter, Congress funded the Special Crisis Intervention Program (P.L. 95-26, ~$200M/yr), allowing direct payments to utilities on behalf of households facing shutoff.
- **1980 — LIEAP:** The Low Income Energy Assistance Program was created under the Crude Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act (P.L. 96-223), a block grant funded at $1.85B for FY1981, emphasizing heating aid to cold-weather states (cooling only for medical need).
- **1981 — LIHEAP established:** Title XXVI of P.L. 97-35 replaced LIEAP effective October 1, 1981, retaining the formula allocation and adding low-cost weatherization as a funded component, with greater state flexibility (including a 25% fund carryover allowance). Authorized at $1.85B/yr for FY1982–84.
- **1984–1994 — Amendments:** The Human Services Reauthorization Acts and the Human Services Amendments of 1994 (P.L. 103-252) refined reporting—most importantly adding the household-reporting requirement in § 2605(c)(1)(G) that underpins today's Household Report.
- **2005 — Performance measurement era:** The Energy Policy Act of 2005 (P.L. 109-58) reauthorized the program and, responding to GPRA-era accountability demands, set the stage for expanded outcome measurement. Following HHS/APPRISE studies (an Energy Burden Study and a Validation Study), **beginning in FY2016** states + DC were required to report four developmental performance measures: the **Benefit Targeting Index**, the **Burden Reduction Targeting Index**, **restoration of home energy service**, and **prevention of service loss**. (For FY2021, the weighted average Benefit Targeting Index was 111—high-burden households received ~11% higher benefits—while the Burden Reduction Index was 86.)
- **Supplemental funding episodes reflected in the data:** The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (2009), the CARES Act (2020, ~$900M), the American Rescue Plan Act (2021, ~$4.5B), and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act all added LIHEAP funds, and the data forms were modified (e.g., ARPA-specific supplemental tables) to track them—important context when comparing years.

---

## 5. Data Content in Detail

**Household Report data elements** (long form): unduplicated counts of assisted households by each assistance type and by ANY type; by poverty interval; by vulnerable group (60+, disabled per state definition, child ≤5); owner/renter status; and counts of applicant households. Instructions emphasize strict unduplicated counting across a state's whole program and cross-checks for consistency against the state's Model Plan and Performance Data Form.

**Performance Data Form:**
- *Module 1 (Grantee Survey, mandatory):* estimated sources and uses of LIHEAP funds, average benefits, and maximum income cutoffs per assistance type. Section III sources are now pre-populated from OCS records.
- *Module 2 (mandatory):* energy burden targeting (income, benefits, energy bills, burden, change in burden) and service restoration/prevention counts.
- *Module 3 (optional):* additional voluntary performance data.

**Report to Congress contents:** fiscal data; home energy data (fuel type/cost/consumption by income group); household data; benefit levels; LIHEAP's offset of average heating costs; vulnerable-household counts; recipiency targeting indices (older adult and young child indices—the older targeting measures); and detailed state tables with footnotes, plus an Appendix A on data collection methodology.

**Data Warehouse tools:** Grant Recipient Profiles (2014–present), Standard Reports, Custom Reports (downloadable tables/graphics), Grantee Search Portal (filter states by eligibility rules, program components, climate zone, fuel type, etc., with CSV export), a published **Inventory of Data Elements**, a glossary, and tutorials. Preliminary FY2025 state data have been uploaded.

---

## 6. Typical Users

1. **Congress and the White House** — oversight, appropriations deliberations, and responses to inquiries (an explicitly stated use).
2. **Federal program managers (OCS/DEA)** — grant monitoring, consistency checks, technical assistance targeting.
3. **State, tribal, and territorial LIHEAP administrators** — benchmarking their programs against peer states (the Grantee Search Portal is explicitly designed for this), program planning, and benefit-matrix design.
4. **Researchers and academics** — studies of energy burden, energy insecurity, poverty, climate adaptation (extreme heat/cold), and public health; APPRISE-published studies are a model.
5. **Advocacy organizations** — e.g., the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), National Consumer Law Center (NCLC), NEUAC—who use the data for appropriations advocacy and to document unmet need (only a fraction of eligible households are served).
6. **Journalists** — coverage of utility shutoffs, heat deaths, and energy affordability.
7. **Utilities and regulators** — low-income program design and arrearage analysis.
8. **Data librarians and preservationists** — see §8.

---

## 7. Benefits to the Public

- **Accountability for ~$4B/yr in federal spending:** the data show where every dollar went, by state and assistance type.
- **Equity evidence:** the vulnerable-population breakdowns (elderly, disabled, young children) and targeting indices document whether aid reaches those most at risk of hypothermia, heat stroke, and utility shutoff.
- **The only comprehensive national source on low-income energy assistance:** no other dataset systematically tracks household-level energy assistance across all states; combined with RECS/ACS linkages, it anchors the national evidence base on "energy burden."
- **Program improvement:** states use peer comparison to redesign benefit matrices and outreach; performance measures push toward outcome (not just output) accountability.
- **Policy design input:** appropriations levels, formula debates (heating vs. cooling state allocations), and climate-resilience policy all draw on this series' 40+ year longitudinal record.

---

## 8. Preservation, Access, and Risk Considerations (for librarians, data scientists, activists)

**Fragility concerns:**
- **April 2025 mass layoffs:** During HHS's April 1, 2025 reduction in force (10,000 staff cut under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.), the **entire staff of the Division of Energy Assistance—roughly 10–25 employees—was terminated**, per reporting by the New York Times, AP, NPR, and others. Advocates (NEADA, NCLC) warned this imperiled ~$378M in undistributed FY2025 funds and the program's future administration, including its data reporting functions. HHS stated it would "continue to comply with" legal obligations. The FY2026 Household Report instructions were subsequently published, indicating reporting infrastructure (much of it contractor-run via APPRISE and OLDC) has continued—but the episode demonstrates that **this data series depends on a very small federal office and is therefore high-risk for disruption**.
- **Publication lag:** the Report to Congress is years behind (FY2022 is the most recent posted), meaning PDF reports are an incomplete mirror of the underlying data; the Data Warehouse is more current but is a **dynamic, JavaScript-driven web application**—not a bulk-downloadable static archive—making web archiving difficult.
- **Format issues:** Reports to Congress are PDFs (tabular data locked in documents); the Warehouse offers CSV export per query but no documented public API or full-database dump. Data scientists will likely need to script extraction or work from the PDF supplemental tables.
- **Contractor dependence:** data compilation, validation, and even website hosting involve contractors (APPRISE); content lives across multiple domains (acf.gov, acf.hhs.gov, liheappm.acf.gov, liheapch.acf.gov, plus the legacy liheapch.ncat.org), complicating comprehensive capture.

**Preservation recommendations:**
1. Archive all Reports to Congress and supplemental table PDFs (they have stable URLs under acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/).
2. Systematically export Data Warehouse Custom Reports across all years (FY2001–present) and all major variable groups to CSV before any infrastructure change.
3. Capture the Inventory of Data Elements, glossaries, Field-by-Field Guides, and annual Household Report/LPDF instructions—these are essential metadata/codebooks without which the numbers are uninterpretable (definitions like "unduplicated count," state-specific disability definitions, and year-specific footnotes matter enormously).
4. Preserve the Action Transmittals (policy guidance) that document year-over-year reporting changes (e.g., treatment of IIJA/ARPA supplemental funds).
5. Note that End of Term Web Archive crawls and data.gov metadata may already hold partial copies.

**Caveats for data users:**
- Reporting coverage differs by grantee type—tribes and territories file abbreviated data and no Performance Data Form, so "national" totals are really "states + DC" for many variables.
- Preliminary vs. final data are both released; revisions occur via OLDC resubmission.
- State definitions (e.g., disability, crisis) vary; cross-state comparisons require the footnoted supplemental tables.
- Unduplicated counting rules changed over time; longitudinal analysis should consult each year's instructions.

---

## 9. Key Sources

- LIHEAP statute compilation (ACF): acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocs/liheap_requirements.pdf
- 45 CFR 96.82 (required household reports): ecfr.gov
- LIHEAP Performance Management site, Data Warehouse, Reports to Congress: liheappm.acf.gov
- CRS, "LIHEAP: Program and Funding" (RL31865): congress.gov
- GAO, "Low-Income Home Energy Assistance: A Program Overview" (HRD-91-1BR)
- Energy Policy Act of 2005 (P.L. 109-58): congress.gov/govinfo
- FY2022 LIHEAP Report to Congress and FY2021 Performance Measures Report (APPRISE)
- News coverage of April 2025 layoffs: NYT (Apr 2, 2025), AP, NPR, The Hill, NCLC

---

**Bottom line:** Your description checks out. This is a statutorily mandated (42 U.S.C. § 8629; 45 CFR 96.82), contractor-supported, grantee-reported data ecosystem spanning 40+ years, with unique value for energy-burden and poverty research—but it is published largely as PDFs and a dynamic web tool, lags several years in its flagship report, and proved acutely vulnerable in 2025 when its entire federal staff was dismissed. It is a strong candidate for proactive archiving.

# Dataset Risk Assessment: LIHEAP Program Data (HHS/ACF/OCS, Division of Energy Assistance)

*Assessment reflects developments through early 2026, including the April 2025 mass termination of LIHEAP staff, the FY2026 budget fight, the November 2025–February 2026 appropriations resolution, and the 2025–2026 OMB paperwork renewals.*

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence per level:**

- **Gone:** No evidence. Data Warehouse (data back to FY2001) is live; Reports to Congress PDFs back many years remain posted at acf.gov and liheappm.acf.gov.
- **High Risk:** No evidence that any prior-year files have been removed.
- **Moderate Risk:** No evidence that prior-year data *elements* have been altered retroactively. (The FY2023–FY2025 data in the Warehouse are flagged "preliminary pending final data validation," which is a processing-status issue, not a removal.)
- **No Known Issue:** All historical series remain accessible: Data Warehouse tables FY2001–present; Grant Recipient Profiles 2014–present; past Reports to Congress posted (liheappm.acf.gov/reports_to_congress, acf.gov/ocs/report/liheap-reports-congress). No known alterations.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Historical files are intact. Caveat for preservationists: the data live in a contractor-supported, JavaScript-driven web application and PDFs rather than a durable bulk archive, so while nothing has been removed, the access mechanism is fragile and worth proactive capture (see prior report).

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence per level:**

- **Gone:** No. Collection continues: FY2025 Household Report instructions issued (preliminary data due Oct 15, 2025; final Dec 31, 2025); FY2025 Performance Data Form guidance published January 27, 2026; a new LIHEAP/RECS data-match collection for FY2024–2025 was noticed in the Federal Register in February and May 2026.
- **High Risk (statutory deadline missed / publication skipped / ICR expired >1 yr):** The statutory Report to Congress deadline (June 30 annually, 42 U.S.C. § 8629(b)) **has been missed repeatedly**: as of early 2026 the most recent published report is **FY2022**—the FY2023 report was due June 30, 2024, and the FY2024 report June 30, 2025. This literally meets the "statutory publication deadline missed" criterion. However, this lateness is chronic and predates the current administration, and the underlying grantee data are still collected and posted (as preliminary) in the Data Warehouse. Both ICRs are active: Household Report (0970-0060) reinstated with change, approved August 10, 2026, expiring August 31, 2029; Performance Data Form (0970-0449) approved through June 30, 2028. No ICR lapse.
- **Moderate Risk:** Publication of the flagship compiled product is delayed by years; FY2023–2025 warehouse data remain "preliminary pending final data validation"—plausibly related to the loss of the validating staff. The FY2025 funding disbursement was delayed ~10 days after the shutdown ended, per Sen. Warren's December 2, 2025 letter.
- **No Known Issue:** ICRs are active and renewed before expiration, and annual grantee collection is on schedule.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Data *collection* is continuing on schedule with valid OMB clearances, and Congress has now funded the program through FY2026. But the statutory compiled publication (Report to Congress) is running 2–3 years behind its statutory deadline, and final validation of recent years is stalled—consistent with a division operating without its dedicated staff. The statutory-deadline-missed language in the rubric's High level is arguably satisfied, but because the underlying data remain available in preliminary form and the delay long predates 2025, Moderate is the better fit; the situation should be re-scored High if FY2023–2024 reports remain unpublished through 2026 or if the FY2026 cycle is skipped.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence per level:**

- **Gone:** No; collection continues.
- **High Risk (actual reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency):** Two documented reductions: **(a) Granularity** — the 2026 Household Report reinstatement (OMB 0970-0060, approved 8/10/2026) explicitly removes the sex, race, and ethnicity sections as "not statutorily required," reversing demographic detail added in 2022; the FY2025 form already replaced gender with "biological sex." **(b) Timeliness** — the Report to Congress series is years behind, and FY2023–2025 warehouse data are stuck in preliminary status.
- **Moderate Risk:** The division that validated grantee submissions (cross-checks against Model Plans, footnoting, consistency review) lost its entire staff in April 2025; Sen. Warren's Dec 2025 letter asks "Who is now responsible for reviewing and posting states' quarterly LIHEAP reports?"—validation capacity is an emerging, unquantified risk.
- **No Known Issue:** Core reporting elements (household counts, poverty intervals, vulnerable-population counts, benefit levels, performance measures) are retained in the renewed ICRs; frequency remains annual.

**Assessment: High Risk.** There are *actual*, OMB-approved reductions in granularity (removal of race/ethnicity/sex demographics from the Household Report) and an actual timeliness reduction (compiled publication years behind; recent cycles unvalidated), not merely potential ones. That said, the core longitudinal series—households served, income levels, vulnerable populations, benefit amounts, targeting indices—remains intact and annual, so this is at the lower end of High.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence per level:**

- **High Risk:** Not applicable—the authorization is neither vague nor substitutable.
- **Moderate Risk:** Not applicable—the collection *is* explicitly required.
- **No Known Issue:** The data collection is **explicitly mandated by statute**: Section 2610 of the LIHEAP statute (42 U.S.C. § 8629) specifies in detail what must be collected (household counts, income levels, fuels, vulnerable-population breakdowns) and requires an annual report to Congress; § 2605(c)(1)(G) and 45 CFR 96.82 require grantee household reports as a condition of receiving funds. No alternative federal data collection substitutes for it (RECS and ACS are supplements, not replacements; they contain no program-administration data). The ICRs themselves cite 42 U.S.C. 8621 and 8629 as authorizing statutes. Congress reaffirmed the program in February 2026 with a $20M funding increase.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** This is one of the most statutorily explicit data collections in the HHS portfolio, with a built-in compliance mechanism (no report, no grant funds). Even the administration that proposed eliminating the program stated it would "continue to comply with statutory requirements."

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence per level:**

- **Gone:** Not fully—program funding continues and some functions are performed by other HHS staff and contractors.
- **High Risk (≥40% staff lost / ≥1,000 lost / budget cut ≥20% / leadership removed):** **100% of the Division of Energy Assistance staff (~23–25 employees) were terminated on April 1, 2025**, including all senior leadership, as part of the HHS RIF of 10,000 (reported by AP, NYT, NPR, The Hill; confirmed by NEADA's Mark Wolfe; protested in bipartisan letters from 13 Senators (Apr 2025), 31 Senators (Nov 2025), and the MA delegation). The division office was effectively dissolved; program administration was transferred to "a small number of other HHS employees" (NEFI, Nov 2025). This exceeds the 40% threshold by the maximum possible margin. The FY2026 President's Budget proposed cutting program funding by **100% (−$4.025B)**.
- **Moderate Risk:** N/A in severity terms—the actual event exceeds Moderate.
- **No Known Issue:** On *appropriated program funding*, Congress rejected the elimination and enacted ~$4.05B for FY2026 (+$20M over FY2025), signed February 2026. The Nov 2025 CR reversed RIFs occurring *during* the shutdown, but reporting indicates the April LIHEAP RIF was not reversed; Warren's Dec 2, 2025 letter was still demanding reinstatement lists and timelines.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The responsible division lost its entire staff and leadership in a single day—this is a textbook High (borderline "Gone" on staffing, mitigated by transfer of functions to other HHS personnel and the contractor-run reporting infrastructure, and by Congress's full restoration of program funding). Administrative (staffing) funding, as opposed to grant funding, remains unaddressed; a bipartisan House bill (Lawler–Gottheimer) to mandate minimum LIHEAP staffing levels has not passed.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence per level:**

- **Gone:** No; collection and publication continue.
- **High Risk (Presidential Action-driven ICR / negative policy note / significant Administration-priority changes):** Multiple direct hits: **(a)** The President's FY2026 Budget (May 2025) proposed terminating LIHEAP with an overtly negative policy justification ("unnecessary," a "pass-through benefitting utilities in the Northeast," citing "fraud and abuse"). **(b)** The FY2025 Household Report was revised to collect "biological sex, rather than gender, in accordance with recent Presidential directives"—a Presidential Action-driven change to the collection instrument. **(c)** The 2026 ICR renewal removes race/ethnicity/sex items, consistent with Administration-wide directives to strip demographic data collections. **(d)** The mass staff termination itself was an Administration restructuring action.
- **Moderate Risk:** Would apply if changes were merely proposed or hinted; here they have been executed.
- **No Known Issue:** Clearly not satisfied—2025 saw some of the most consequential changes in the program's 44-year history.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The dataset has been directly reshaped by Presidential directives (demographic data elements removed), and the Administration formally proposed eliminating the underlying program. The principal mitigating fact—Congress's bipartisan rejection of elimination and $20M increase in February 2026—reduces the likelihood of near-term termination but does not undo the policy-driven changes already made to the data instruments.

---

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **No Known Issue** | FY2001–present warehouse data and past reports all remain posted; no removals detected. |
| **Future Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** | Collection and ICRs current (through 2028–2029), but statutory Report to Congress deadline missed by 2–3 years and FY2023–25 data stuck in preliminary status. |
| **Data Quality** | **High Risk** | OMB-approved removal of race/ethnicity/sex data elements; compiled publication timeliness severely degraded; validation capacity lost with staff. |
| **Statutory Context** | **No Known Issue** | Explicitly mandated (42 U.S.C. § 8629; 45 CFR 96.82); detailed statutory specification; no substitutes; funding reaffirmed. |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **High Risk** | 100% of Division of Energy Assistance staff (~23–25) terminated April 1, 2025; leadership removed; administration proposed 100% budget cut—though Congress ultimately increased grant funding. |
| **Policy** | **High Risk** | President's budget proposed elimination; instruments revised per Presidential directive (gender→sex; demographics stripped); program openly criticized by the Administration. |

**Overall:** LIHEAP data present an unusual risk profile—*legally and congressionally well-anchored, but administratively decapitated*. The statute, the compliance lever (no report, no funds), bipartisan appropriations support, and contractor-run infrastructure have kept the data flowing; but the people who validated, compiled, and published it are gone, its flagship publication is years behind, its demographic content has been politically curtailed, and the Administration has formally sought the program's elimination once already. Preservationists should treat the current accessibility of the full historical series as an opportunity to archive now, while monitoring the FY2026 reporting cycle, the fate of the stalled Report to Congress series, and any FY2027 budget request for renewed elimination proposals.
